newsitem.title: UK: British business wants simple budget for long-term.
newsitem.headline: British business wants simple budget for long-term.

text.p: Businesses across Britain would like to see Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown deliver a simple budget which takes a long-term view, but fear his need to raise revenue may lead to higher taxes on companies.

Many firms fear Brown's first budget on July 2 will seek to raise money by cutting advance corporation tax (ACT) or property relief, raising inheritance tax or introducing "green" taxes, which all could hit small businesses.

Elizabeth Haywood, director of the Wales branch of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) in Swansea, said she wanted a budget with no big surprises but hoped for some gentle measures to curb consumer demand.

"If there has to be some fiscal tightening, we need to have it in the personal taxation end rather than the business taxation end," Haywood said, noting that increasing corporation tax would not affect consumer demand.

Firms are worried that if the budget fails to produce adequate fiscal tightening targeted at the personal sector, the Bank of England will tighten monetary policy aggressively to avoid a resurgence in inflation.

Prime Minister Tony Blair called at a United Nations environmental summit in New York this week for sweeping lifestyle changes to reduce greenhouse emissions, fuelling speculation the budget may contain new "green" taxes on petrol, diesel and car use.
Haywood said this would hit the Welsh economy as it relies heavily on road freight.

Tom Alexander, a tax adviser at Belfast chartered accountants Goldblatt McGuigan, said Brown had to raise money but should avoid obvious tax raises that would hurt the large number of small companies in Northern Ireland.

Alexander would be concerned about measures such as raising the age limit on retirement relief, reduction of property relief to 50 percent from 100 percent and changes in rules on residence for tax purposes and offshore tax avoidance.
"ACT is one measure which will require a bit of care because it has a huge implications in international investment terms," Alexander said.

Firms pay ACT on their dividend payments in advance to cover shareholders' tax liabilities and can then deduct the money from their corporation tax bill. Tax-exempt shareholders can then claim a refund on the dividend tax paid on their behalf.
"In relation to pension funds receiving dividends, there is high speculation that they will get no credit whatsoever," he said. This would make investing in shares less attractive.
Analysts estimate that full abolition of ACT would save the Treasury around five billion pounds a year, while reducing it by half to 10 percent should garner nearly three billion stg.
Like Haywood, Alexander fears a rise in green taxes would hit the local economy hard.
Geoff Edwards, a partner at accountants Grant Thornton, which advises around 100 small owner-managed businesses in central England, said ACT was a concern for many of his clients.

"Their major concerns have been to do with what that will do to them when they are paying dividends out and what that might do to the expectations of institutions, particularly pension funds," he said.

"There is also quite a bit of concern...that higher rate relief might be withdrawn from pension schemes and where they do not have a company pension scheme and are paying for their own individual scheme," he said.
"Quite a lot of money seems to be moving into the individual schemes in anticipation of a change."
Firms that were moving property also feared an increase in stamp duty and many were rushing to finalise tax plans ahead of a suspected reduction in retirement relief and inheritance tax.
But despite the last minute rush, Edwards said he expected the budget to be a long term "tax manifesto".

John Downie, a research officer at the Federation of Small Businesses, which represents 100,000 businesses across Britain, said he wanted to see incentives for small firms to reinvest more of their profits.

Downie said 97 percent of UK firms employed 20 people or under. Brown should introduce a scheme to allow these companies to hold onto more of their profits if they pledged to plough the capital back into the business.
"It would promote employment and more investment... and that will benefit the economy," he said, adding that it would fit neatly into Brown's pledge to fight long term unemployment.

Paul Bartlett, the manager of a small scale construction machinery import and export business in the West Country, said he would like to see Brown tackle the spiralling strength of sterling. "What is crippling our business is the strength of the pound," he said.
The pound's 19 percent appreciation since last August was directly responsible for turning his 200,000 pound a month business into a 50,000 pound a month business.
Any rise in petrol taxes would be a further blow as his business requires a good deal of travelling.
